newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: U.S., Britain promise help for Kabila's New Congo.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Britain promise help for Kabila's New Congo.

text.p: Ambassadors from the United States and Britain congratulated self-proclaimed President Laurent Kabila in the Democratic Republic of Congo and promised their support, national television said on Sunday.

The television said the ambassadors, both from countries accused by ousted President Mobutu Sese Seko's government of backing the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (AFDL), met Kabila on Saturday.

"We brought congratulations to President Kabila for the victory won by the Alliance in Kinshasa, above all we congratulated the president for having succeeded in this victory with a minimum of losses," U.S. Ambassador Daniel Simpson said.

It was the first time Simpson had met Kabila since his troops captured Kinshasa last weekend after a seven-month rebellion. But he had already met the then rebel leader at his southern headquarters in Lubumbashi.
"We are going to send a team of representatives from our different ministries...to establish contacts with the new authorities here. That will be in the coming days," Simpson said.

Mobutu was a Cold War ally of the United States as a bastion of support against Soviet communist expansion in Africa, but with the fall of the Berlin Wall the U.S. began to accuse him of human rights abuses and corruption.
Officials in the Moroccan capital Rabat said Mobutu, weakened by cancer, would be heading for exile in France after arriving in Morocco from Togo on Friday.
Western countries have welcomed the toppling of Mobutu and his entourage, who were widely accused of pillaging what is potentially one of Africa's richest nations and amassing personal fortunes.

But they have made their support conditional on Kabila's formation of a broad-based government to steer Africa's third largest country to multi-party elections -- a transition Mobutu reluctantly agreed to and then failed to implement.

Kabila told U.S.-based television network CNN during a little-publicised visit to a Kinshasa hospital on Saturday the country had to prepare for elections but said there would be a "democratic election after (a) two years transitional period".

The British Ambassador to Kinshasa, Marcus Hope, said Britain wanted to cooperate with the new government in Congo and hoped to be able to help out in areas of stability, elections and economic development.
"I brought a message from my prime minister who wants to see the possibilities of cooperating with the government," Hope told the television.

Both Britain and the United States have close relations with Congo's eastern neighbours Uganda and Rwanda, which according to Western intelligence and Congo sources supplied troops to help fight the civil war.

On Saturday Alliance troops stopped a demonstration by around 1,000 students against the exclusion from Kabila's government of popular Mobutu-era opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi and against the presence of foreign troops.
